name: Ventus-Erratum
specific_features: Sand formations that mimic artificial structures
description: Ventus-Erratum is a world shaped entirely by wind, its surface an art gallery of natural erosion where sandstone has been carved into formations of such delicate improbability that early surveyors mistook them for artificial constructions. Rock arches span canyons with seemingly impossible grace, their spans thinned to translucent sheets by millennia of abrasive wind. Mesa formations rise from flat desert plains like the ruins of ancient citadels, their layered profiles recording changing wind patterns across geological time.

The wind never stops on Ventus-Erratum. The thin atmosphere moves in planet-spanning circulation patterns that drive dust devil corridors along predictable paths, columns of spinning sand that march across the desert in formations that can stretch to the horizon. The wind carries a fine abrasive grit that etches exposed surfaces with remarkable speed, polishing metal to mirror brightness and eroding stone into curves and hollows. Sound is the constant companion of anyone on the surface: the whistle and moan of air through rock formations creates an eerie symphony that shifts with wind speed and direction.

Despite thorough survey work, no evidence of life has been found on Ventus-Erratum, past or present. The planet appears to have been dry since its formation, its water never condensing from the primordial atmosphere before being stripped away by solar wind. The sand formations that mimic artificial structures are the product of erosion patterns following mineral vein geometries, natural processes that coincidentally produce right angles and regular spacings. This has not prevented persistent popular belief that the formations are remnants of an ancient civilization.

Mining operations target the rare earth elements exposed by erosion in the mineral veins, deposits that would normally lie deep underground but have been conveniently brought to the surface by billions of years of wind work. The challenge is that the same wind that exposed the deposits also destroys extraction equipment with relentless abrasion. Sealed and hardened machinery lasts months rather than years, and everything exposed to the wind develops a characteristic polish that miners call the Erratum shine. The planet's austere beauty draws occasional tourists despite the discomfort, visitors who come to see the rock arches and stay to listen to the wind.
